author.name: Bidisha Bhattacharyya
author.tagline: Stories that linger long after the last page.
author.heroSupporting: Welcome to the literary world of Bidisha Bhattacharyya, an independent author, poet and creative writer from West Bengal, India. Exploring horror, suspense, romance, poetry and the many emotions that make us human, her writing brings imagination and storytelling together.
author.locationNote: Earlier 2022 records cite Barrackpore, West Bengal (author confirmation recommended)

author.workingBio:
Bidisha Bhattacharyya is an independent author, fiction writer, poet and creative professional from West Bengal, India.

Her literary interests span multiple genres, including horror, suspense, fantasy, romance, poetry, haiku, flash fiction and short stories.

Her writing journey began through online platforms such as YourQuote and Wattpad. Following her Class 12 examinations, writing gradually developed into a stronger passion, encouraging her to explore different forms of creative expression.

Through reading, practice and creative learning, she developed an interest in storytelling across different formats.

Alongside her literary work, Bidisha has explored professional writing, copywriting, blogging and promotional content.

Her creative journey continues through books, literary contributions and professional projects.

author.quote: Writing is not merely about arranging words; it is about summoning the quiet shadows, unsaid desires, and haunting truths that echo in the human soul.

writingPhilosophy.heading: Beyond Words, There Are Worlds.
writingPhilosophy.text: Every story begins with an idea. Every poem begins with a feeling. And every page creates an opportunity to see the world differently.

writingSamples.title: The Mirror in the Attics
writingSamples.excerpt: It wasn't that the glass was cracked. It was that when she turned her back to walk down the narrow cedar stairs, the reflection remained standing — smiling with teeth that were not hers.
writingSamples.fullText:
It wasn't that the glass was cracked. It was that when she turned her back to walk down the narrow cedar stairs, the reflection remained standing — smiling with teeth that were not hers.

For three decades, the attic of the ancestral manor in Barrackpore had been bolted shut with brass padlocks whose keys had dissolved into rumor. But damp monsoon winds have a way of unmaking old iron. The door had swollen, then yielded with a groan that sounded entirely too human.

Inside, dust hung like suspended memory. She had only meant to retrieve the cedar chest of handwritten letters. Instead, her lantern caught the silvered edges of the Venetian mirror.

She took one step forward. The mirror took two. And in the silence between breaths, a voice like dry leaves whispered from behind the glass: 'You took forty years to return. I have stayed hungry every single day.'

writingSamples.title: Three Breaths of Monsoon
writingSamples.excerpt: Rain knocks on the pane, / words we never dared to say / drown beneath the dark.
writingSamples.fullText:
Rain knocks on the pane, 
Words we never dared to say 
Drown beneath the dark.

* * *

Ink on brittle page, 
Old letters carry your voice 
Through an empty room.

* * *

Midnight strikes again, 
The heart learns what quiet means 
When the shadows stay.

writingSamples.title: The Anatomy of a Secret
writingSamples.excerpt: Trust is like bone china in a tempest: you can piece the shards together with molten gold, but the fractures will forever remember where the impact struck.
writingSamples.fullText:
Trust is like bone china in a tempest: you can piece the shards together with molten gold, but the fractures will forever remember where the impact struck.

She folded the telegram three times, sliding it into the hollow lining of her coat. If he found it, the evening would dissolve into accusations; if he didn't, the silence would poison them both by sunrise.

Marriage in high society was not built on confession; it was maintained by the artful omission of dangerous truths. But tonight, outside the frosted window panes, a car engine had idled for twenty-five minutes without headlights.

Whoever was sitting inside that vehicle wasn't waiting for an invitation. They were waiting for a signal.

writingSamples.title: Pieces That Stay
writingSamples.excerpt: We collect ourselves from the edges of people who could only hold us for a season, and we call the mending poetry.
writingSamples.fullText:
We collect ourselves 
from the edges of people 
who could only hold us for a season, 
and we call the mending poetry.

There are nights when sorrow 
feels like an ancient riverbed 
carved into the ribcage, 
deep enough to hold every tear 
you swore you would never cry again.

Yet the sun returns, 
unhurried and unforgiving, 
to remind the soil: 
even the broken ground 
learns how to bloom.

writingSamples.title: The Threshold at Midnight
writingSamples.excerpt: Every family has a room that everyone pretends does not exist until the floorboards begin to creak in the small hours.
writingSamples.fullText:
Every family has a room that everyone pretends does not exist until the floorboards begin to creak in the small hours.

In our household, it was the corner chamber past the pantry where grandfather's clocks were kept. Seven pendulum clocks, each wound to a different hour, ticking in a polyrhythmic chorus that drowned out the night frogs.

On the night before my departure for the university, I found Aunt Maya standing before the tallest mahogany clock. Her fingers were pressed flat against the glass casing, tracing the pendulum's frantic arc.

'Do not come back after dusk,' she said without turning. 'When you leave this house, remember: the past does not run backward, but it knows how to wait.'

writingSamples.title: On the Architecture of Solitude
writingSamples.excerpt: Solitude is not the absence of company; it is the presence of an unfiltered self demanding honesty.
writingSamples.fullText:
Solitude is not the absence of company; it is the presence of an unfiltered self demanding honesty.

When I write, the world outside fades into gentle murmurs. The characters who step into the light of the desk lamp bring their own shadows, their unhealed wounds, their stubborn yearnings. To be a writer is to hold vigil for voices that have no other throat through which to speak.

We build worlds out of twenty-six letters, hoping that somewhere across miles of silence, a stranger turns the page and whispers: 'I thought I was the only one.'
